To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the stimulus‐related changes in the fMRI signal have a complex space‐time structure; (ii) the non‐stimulusrrelated changes in the signal correspond in detail to respiration and the heartbeat; and (iii) the signal also contains low frequency oscillations with frequencies of about 0.1Hz which are likely to originate from the vascular system.
the hemodynamic response to a simple visual stimulus is not a single event but rather a complex spatiomorphological pattern of changes in the brain.

functional magnetic resonance imaging is a complex phenomenon, which is not only due to changes in blood oxygenation, but also due to changes in cerebral hemodynamic parameters, and that the changes are spatiotemporally complex even for the simplest visual stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and sources of the noise in functional magnetic resonance images.
the development of methods for the study of the nature of the hemodynamic changes in the brain, and their relation to the neural activity.
the nature of spatiatemporal changes in functional magnetic resonance images.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stimulus related signal in the fMRI time series has a very complex structure, which cannot be explained by simple linear superposition.
the stimulus‐induced changes in blood flow are superimposed on a complex spatiatemporal background of physiological origin.
the stimulus related hemodynamic changes are superimposed on the nontrivial spatiotemporally structured background of the hemodynamics of the human brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in functional MR imaging are complex and cannot be described in a simple way.
the changes in the images can be separated into three categories: (a) stimulus related, (b) breathing, and (c) heart beat.

the hemodynamic response to a stimulus is not simply an impulse response, but a complex, spatiotemporally structured process, which is likely to be the result of a combination of vasodilation and vasoconstriction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in addition to stimulus‐related changes, there are other, stimulus independent changes in the image that are of a similar magnitude and that are also spatially structured, which must be taken into account for the analysis of functional magnetic resonance images.
the hemodynamic response is a complex, spatiotemporally nonstationary process, which should be taken into account when analyzing functional magnetic resonance imaging data.

the nature of changes in functional magnetic resonance images is far more complex than has been appreciated in the literature, and that the use of denoising and spectral techniques is necessary to reveal this complexity.
